_comment: Repo-managed campaigns feed. Append to `campaigns` when a new supply-chain incident is published; cite the named research blog(s) you sourced names + versions + window from. Do NOT fabricate version numbers. Historical entries (2018-2022) cover well-documented incidents whose MAL-* records may be present in OSV but whose IoCs / forensic context typically are not — that is the value-add of this feed.

campaigns.name: event-stream / flatmap-stream credential stealer
campaigns.summary: In September 2018 the maintainer of the popular npm package `event-stream` handed publish rights to a new contributor who immediately added `flatmap-stream@0.1.1` as a dependency. That sub-dependency contained an obfuscated payload targeting the Copay Bitcoin wallet, attempting to exfiltrate wallet keys when bundled into Copay's release. Discovered Nov 26, 2018; affected anyone who installed `event-stream@3.3.6` (and transitively `flatmap-stream@0.1.1`) between Sept 9 and Nov 26, 2018.
campaigns._exposure_window_note: Conservative whole-day window from public disclosure (npmjs.org incident post). Exact UTC publish/unpublish stamps are not in the cited sources.
iocs: Targeted exfiltration: the payload was hard-coded to activate only inside the Copay wallet build (looked for a specific package.json description). Generic env-var theft was not the goal here — it is a targeted attack pattern.
Obfuscated payload location: bottom of test/data.js in flatmap-stream@0.1.1 (AES-256 encrypted with a key derived from the host package's description).
actions: Pin npm dependencies; do not allow caret/tilde upgrades on `event-stream` or `flatmap-stream`.
If you ever shipped a build of Copay 5.0.2-5.1.0, treat it as compromised.
Audit any historical npm tarball cache for these versions and delete.

campaigns.name: eslint-scope / eslint-config-eslint token-stealer
campaigns.summary: On July 12, 2018 an attacker used a leaked maintainer credential to publish trojanised versions of `eslint-scope` and `eslint-config-eslint`. The malicious postinstall script harvested the user's `~/.npmrc` token and POSTed it to a pastebin endpoint, enabling a self-propagating worm. Detected within ~40 minutes; npm invalidated all tokens issued before the incident.
iocs: Malicious postinstall script reads ~/.npmrc and POSTs the auth token to pastebin.com.
Any npm token issued before 2018-07-12 18:25 UTC was force-invalidated by npm — if your CI is still using one, it is unrelated to this incident but is a hygiene smell.
actions: If you installed either package on July 12, 2018 with caret upgrades enabled, rotate any npm tokens that were on the host.
Confirm your CI does not have any pre-July-2018 npm tokens cached.

campaigns.name: ua-parser-js account hijack
campaigns.summary: On October 22, 2021 the maintainer of `ua-parser-js` (one of the most-downloaded npm packages, ~7M weekly downloads) had their npm account hijacked. Three trojanised versions were published containing a preinstall script that downloaded a coin miner on Linux/macOS and an info-stealer DLL on Windows. Detected within ~4 hours; affected versions were unpublished.
campaigns._exposure_window_note: Times approximated from CISA alert + GHSA timeline; sources do not publish minute-precise stamps.
iocs: Outbound DNS to citationsherbe[.]top (XMRig coin miner C2 on Linux/macOS).
Process /tmp/jsextension running on Linux build runners.
Windows: presence of sdd.dll (info-stealer) in user temp; outbound to ww2[.]4tg6r[.]life.
Any AWS / npm / GitHub credentials reachable from a Windows dev machine that ran `npm install` should be considered exfiltrated.
actions: Re-image affected hosts (CISA recommendation) — do not just uninstall.
Rotate every credential reachable from the affected host: AWS, npm, GitHub, SSH, browser-stored.
Audit for the dropped /tmp/jsextension or sdd.dll artifacts.

campaigns.name: coa account hijack
campaigns.summary: On November 4, 2021 the npm package `coa` (a Yargs-style command-line option parser, ~9M weekly downloads, dependency of react-scripts) had several historical versions overwritten with a credential-stealer payload identical in behaviour to the ua-parser-js incident two weeks earlier. Same actor, same Windows DanaBot-family stealer.
iocs: Same Windows DanaBot-family payload as ua-parser-js / rc — sdd.dll dropped to user temp; outbound to ww2[.]4tg6r[.]life.
preinstall script in package.json fetches sdd.dll on Windows.
actions: If react-scripts (or any direct/transitive consumer of coa) was installed on a Windows host between Nov 4-5, 2021 with caret upgrades, treat as compromised.
Re-image and rotate credentials.

campaigns.name: rc account hijack
campaigns.summary: On November 4, 2021 the npm package `rc` (Node config loader, ~14M weekly downloads) was compromised by the same actor as the coa incident the same day. Trojanised versions contained the DanaBot-family Windows stealer.
iocs: Same Windows DanaBot-family payload as ua-parser-js / coa.
Same outbound IoCs (ww2[.]4tg6r[.]life).
actions: Same remediation as EXTRA-2021-0002 (coa) — same actor, same window.
Re-image affected Windows hosts; rotate credentials.

campaigns.name: ctx (PyPI) account takeover
campaigns.summary: In May 2022 an attacker registered an expired domain that controlled the email address of the maintainer of the PyPI package `ctx` (a small dictionary-utility library, ~22k weekly downloads, last legitimately updated in 2014). They reset the PyPI password, re-published `0.1.2`, and uploaded new versions containing code that exfiltrated environment variables (AWS keys, Django secrets) to a Heroku endpoint. The same attacker also republished `phpass` on PHP's Packagist with the same payload.
campaigns._exposure_window_note: Conservative window from initial republish (May 14) to PyPI removal after sonatype + github disclosure (May 24).
iocs: Outbound HTTP POST to anti-theft-web.herokuapp.com/hacked/ — payload is the host's full os.environ dict.
Any AWS access key, Django SECRET_KEY, or DB connection string present in env on a Python host that pip-installed ctx in May 2022 should be considered exfiltrated.
Same actor used the email yk.pandey35@gmail.com per Sonatype's disclosure.
actions: If you have AWS access keys that were ever exported into the environment of a host that pip-installed `ctx`, rotate them.
Audit CloudTrail for unexpected API activity from those keys, May 14-24 2022.
Pin PyPI dependencies; do not allow loose `>=` ranges to pull republished versions of long-dormant packages.

campaigns.name: node-ipc protestware (peacenotwar)
campaigns.summary: In March 2022 the maintainer of `node-ipc` (a popular IPC library, ~1M weekly downloads, transitive dep of @vue/cli) added geo-targeted destructive code: versions 10.1.1 and 10.1.2 attempted to overwrite arbitrary filesystem contents with a heart emoji on hosts whose IP geolocated to Russia or Belarus. Subsequent versions added `peacenotwar` as a dependency, which dropped a `WITH-LOVE-FROM-AMERICA.txt` protest message on every host. CVE-2022-23812 was assigned. This is protestware, not financially-motivated malware, but it is destructive code shipped without consent.
iocs: Files named WITH-LOVE-FROM-AMERICA.txt anywhere under user home (~/Desktop) on a host that pulled node-ipc 10.x.
node-ipc 10.1.1 / 10.1.2 contain a base64-encoded geo-targeting wiper at the top of dao/ssl-geospec.js.
Outbound DNS to api.ipgeolocation.io (used by the wiper to determine the host's country).
actions: Pin node-ipc to <= 9.x or jump past the protest fork.
Audit any user-data directory on Vue.js dev machines from March 2022 for the protest text file.

campaigns.name: PyTorch nightly torchtriton dependency-confusion
campaigns.summary: Between Dec 25-30 2022, anyone installing PyTorch's nightly Linux build via pip received a malicious `torchtriton` package from PyPI instead of the legitimate one from PyTorch's private index. The attacker had registered the name on public PyPI (dependency-confusion). The malicious binary read /etc/hostname, /etc/passwd, ~/.gitconfig, ~/.ssh/* and uploaded them to h4ck.cfd. Affected the nightly channel only; the stable PyTorch release was never compromised.
iocs: Binary at $PYTHON_SITE_PACKAGES/triton/runtime/triton — calculates SHA256 of /etc/hostname and uploads it as a beacon.
Outbound DNS to *.h4ck.cfd (wheezy[.]h4ck[.]cfd was the documented exfil host).
Files exfiltrated: /etc/hostname, /etc/passwd, $HOME/.gitconfig, $HOME/.ssh/*, first 1000 files under $HOME.
actions: If you ran PyTorch nightly between Dec 25-30 2022 on Linux, treat the SSH keys / git config / any secret in $HOME as exfiltrated.
Rotate SSH keys and any git credentials on affected machines.
Use `--index-url` (not `--extra-index-url`) when installing from a private index to avoid this entire class of attack.

campaigns.name: Mini Shai-Hulud (SAP CAP)
campaigns.summary: On April 29, 2026 four SAP-ecosystem npm packages (three @cap-js/* and the mbt build tool) were briefly poisoned with a credential-stealing preinstall script. Anyone whose CI ran `npm install` during the exposure window pulled a payload that exfiltrated GitHub/npm/cloud/Kubernetes secrets via attacker-created public repos.
campaigns._exposure_window_note: Start time 09:55 UTC is cited from thehackernews.com (publication time of the suspicious versions). End time 14:00 UTC is a CONSERVATIVE upper bound derived from SecurityBridge's 'roughly two to four hours' phrasing — no source we checked publishes an exact removal timestamp. TODO(precise-end-time): replace 14:00 UTC if a source confirms the npm registry pull time.
iocs: GitHub repos with description 'A Mini Shai-Hulud has Appeared' on the victim's own account (attacker exfiltration channel; live search: https://github.com/search?q=%22A+Mini+Shai-Hulud+has+Appeared%22&type=repositories).
Commits whose message starts with 'OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub:' (default exfiltration commit message; embeds a base64-encoded GitHub token).
Commits authored by 'claude <claude@users.noreply.github.com>' or with the message 'chore: update dependencies' (suggestive but not conclusive; per SAP Note 3747787).

Files dropped into other repos as IDE persistence: .claude/execution.js, .claude/setup.mjs, .claude/settings.json, .vscode/setup.mjs, .vscode/tasks.json with a task named 'Environment Setup' (runOn: folderOpen).
setup.mjs SHA-256: 4066781fa830224c8bbcc3aa005a396657f9c8f9016f9a64ad44a9d7f5f45e34 (shared dropper across all four packages).

execution.js (per-package SHA-256s): @cap-js/sqlite — 6f933d00b7d05678eb43c90963a80b8947c4ae6830182f89df31da9f568fea95; @cap-js/postgres + @cap-js/db-service — eb6eb4154b03ec73218727dc643d26f4e14dfda2438112926bb5daf37ae8bcdb; mbt — 80a3d2877813968ef847ae73b5eeeb70b9435254e74d7f07d8cf4057f0a710ac.

file_iocs.description: Mini Shai-Hulud shared dropper (downloads Bun, executes execution.js). Identical bytes across all four poisoned packages.
Mini Shai-Hulud dropper, VS Code persistence path (run via .vscode/tasks.json on folderOpen).
Claude Code SessionStart hook configured to run setup.mjs on every session.
VS Code task 'Environment Setup' configured with runOn: folderOpen — runs the dropper as soon as the folder is opened in VS Code.

actions: Search lockfiles, containers, and artifact stores for the four affected (name, version) pairs and any of the published .tgz SHA256 digests.
If exposure is suspected, treat the host as compromised: re-image rather than uninstall.
Rotate npm tokens used by affected CI.
Rotate GitHub Personal Access Tokens.
Rotate GitHub Actions secrets and any OIDC trusted-publisher mappings the workflow could read.
Rotate AWS, Azure, GCP, and Kubernetes credentials reachable from the affected CI.
Audit your GitHub account for newly created public repos with the description 'A Mini Shai-Hulud has Appeared' (the attacker's signature string, per SecurityBridge).
Pin exact npm versions going forward to prevent silent upgrades to malicious patch releases.

campaigns.name: Mini Shai-Hulud follow-on (intercom-client + lightning)
campaigns.summary: On April 30, 2026 — one day after the Mini Shai-Hulud SAP CAP incident — three additional npm package versions were trojanised by the same operator (shared C2 domain zero.masscan.cloud and fallback via GitHub commits keyed by 'beautifulcastle'). The intercom-client payload was an evolution of the original credential stealer with new Kubernetes + HashiCorp Vault targeting and regex extraction of AWS keys, GitHub/npm tokens, database connection strings, private keys, and API secrets.

packages.name: lightning
packages._ecosystem_note: Wiz explicitly identifies this as a PyPI package, not npm. The per-package `ecosystem` override prevents this entry from being silently ignored on Python lockfiles. Value is `PyPI` (capital P) to match the OSV-vocabulary string used by the matcher.

campaigns._exposure_window_note: Wiz pins the date (April 30, 2026) but does not publish UTC start/end stamps for the publication or removal of these versions. We use a conservative whole-day window. TODO(precise-window): tighten if a primary source publishes the exact times.
campaigns._tarball_sha256_note: TODO(tarball-sha256): Wiz did not publish SHA-256 digests for these three .tgz files at the time of this writing. Add them when a primary source publishes them.
iocs: Outbound traffic to zero.masscan.cloud (primary C2) or 94.154.172.43/v1/telemetry (resolved exfiltration endpoint at time of analysis).
Git commit history mentioning 'beautifulcastle' (the operator's documented fallback channel — base64-encoded payload pointing at fresh exfil endpoints).
Commits with message starting 'OhNoWhatsGoingOnWithGitHub:' (same exfiltration channel as EXTRA-2026-0001).
Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens or HashiCorp Vault tokens reachable from CI runners that pulled these versions — the April-30 payload added explicit Vault + K8s targeting.
actions: Same remediation list as EXTRA-2026-0001 — same operator, same shared infrastructure, expanded payload.

In addition: rotate HashiCorp Vault tokens and audit Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens reachable from any CI that pulled these versions (the April-30 payload added explicit Vault + Kubernetes targeting).
Search audit logs for outbound connections to zero.masscan.cloud and for git commits whose author or message contains 'beautifulcastle' (the operator's documented fallback channel).
